Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review relevant thoracic spine anatomy.
Discuss the etiology of thoracic disk herniations and degenerative pathology.
Recognize appropriate imaging studies for thoracic level herniations and stenosis.
Review treatment options for the management of symptomatic thoracic level compression.
Pathoanatomy/Pathophysiology
Definition and demographics
Degenerative changes in the thoracic spine lead to disk herniations and stenosis.
Disk abnormalities are common, and most patients with a disk abnormality are
asymptomatic.



Thoracic disk herniations contribute to 0.04% to 4% of symptomatic herniations and 1% of
surgical procedures for the management of herniated disks.1
Affects older individuals1
Affects men and women equally1
Overview

Overview
Symptomatic thoracic level compression from degenerative changes is uncommon. Disk
herniations and stenosis in the thoracic spine are associated with common symptoms,
including back pain, and may result in signs and symptoms of neurologic compression.
Thoracic stenosis requiring surgical management is more rare than cervical and lumbar
stenosis; however, given the potential for spinal cord level involvement, thoracic stenosis
must be considered to avoid incorrect or delayed diagnosis.
Epidemiology
Symptomatic thoracic stenosis and disk herniations are rare.
Surgical management rarely is necessary.

Epidemiology
Although the incidence of thoracic stenosis is difficult to determine, thoracic stenosis
may contribute to as many as 1% of all disk herniations.1-3 Radiographic studies indicate
that as many as 73% of asymptomatic individuals have some thoracic disk abnormalities
that can be detected on MRI.1-5 Males and females are affected at equal rates, and
symptoms begin later in life, generally in patients in their thirties to fifties.6-8 Surgical
management of symptomatic thoracic disk disease is rare and accounts for less than 2%
of all surgical procedures for the management of symptomatic disk herniations.4,9-11

Although MRI has improved the detection of thoracic herniations, most thoracic
herniations are detected via radiography and are of little clinical importance.12
Natural History
Most patients return to normal activity.
Lower extremity symptoms may portend poorer outcomes.

Natural History
Limited evidence is available on the natural history of disk herniations in the thoracic
spine. A study of 55 patients reported return to prior level of activity in 78% treated
nonsurgcially.5 Lower extremity symptoms or dysfunction suggest more severe disease.
Patients with these symptoms often experience progression, with a higher proportion
undergoing surgical treatment.7 Younger patients with a history of trauma initially report
back pain and may experience a more rapid progression of myelopathy. Older patients
with considerably more degeneration will initially report a much slower course of
symptoms that corresponds with the degenerative nature of their pathology.2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The thoracic spine consists of 12 vertebral bodies with paired facet joints for respective ribs.
Thoracic canal diameter is small, and most of the canal space is occupied by the spinal cord.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Twelve vertebrae compose the thoracic spine. Specific distinguishing factors differentiate
the thoracic spine from the remainder of the axial skeleton. Thoracic facet joints are
relatively coronal in orientation and gradually transition to a more sagittal orientation at
the levels of the thoracolumbar junction. Notably, each thoracic vertebra contains paired
facets on the lateral aspects that provide an articulation between the vertebra and its
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM
AAOS | Thoracic Disk Herniations and Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053
3/27

corresponding rib head. The thoracic spine receives additional stability from the rib cage
in multiple axes of rotation, specifically flexion and rotation.13 In addition, the cross-
sectional diameter of the thoracic canal is smaller than that of the cervical and lumbar
canals.14 The decrease in available space for the spinal cord may become problematic
and explains how a relatively small space-occupying lesion may result in symptomatic
compression of neural elements.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Degenerative change is the most common cause of thoracic stenosis.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Intervertebral disk degeneration that results from increasing age leads to changes in disk
architecture, including weakening and tearing of the anulus and loss of hydration of the
disk matrix. Annular tears create areas where disk contents can migrate into the canal.1
Neurologic injury results from direct compression and vascular insult.2,7,15,16 Case
reports and autopsy studies have shown distortion of the spinal cord at the
corresponding level of thoracic disk herniations and patent vasculature.17 In patients
who have an atypical presentation with unusual or unexpected deficits, such as transient
plegia, vascular injury or insufficiency is implicated.7
The role of trauma in patients with a thoracic herniated disk is controversial. As many as
60% of patients may report a history of trauma.18 Identifying the true cause via mere
coincidence may be a challenge. Inciting events may include simple bending, twisting, or
lifting or high-energy impact.
Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM
AAOS | Thoracic Disk Herniations and Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053
4/27

Thoracic disk herniations and thoracic stenosis are most common in patients in their thirties to
fifties.

Risk Factors
The concept that thoracic stenosis is an age-related diagnosis is supported by evidence
demonstrating that the likelihood of thoracic disk herniations is highest in the
thoracolumbar spine, which is an area of higher stress. Imaging studies have identified
higher rates of osteophyte formation and disk degeneration at these levels.19-21
Classification
Although no clear standardized classification system for thoracic intervertebral disk
degeneration exists, degenerative changes that become symptoms generally are categorized
as one of three diagnoses.
Spondylosis

Spondylosis
The thoracic spine is subject to intervertebral disk degeneration. As disks degenerate,
their load-bearing capabilities are reduced, and a greater amount of force is distributed
to the surrounding ligaments and facets. Over time, thoracic facets degenerate, and
degenerative changes similar to those in other cartilaginous joints are observed.
Degeneration leads to osteophyte formation, ligamentum thickening and redundancy,
and facet overgrowth. As the spine degenerates, a greater degree of spondylosis is
observed. In patients without neural compression, degeneration is asymptomatic.
Instability secondary to degeneration is rare given the stability provided by the ribs.5
Stenosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM
AAOS | Thoracic Disk Herniations and Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053
5/27


Stenosis
Narrowing of the spinal canal may result from degeneration and is termed stenosis. In
the few available studies on the surgical management of thoracic stenosis, results
generally are poorer than those of the surgical management of cervical or lumbar
stenosis. Palumbo et al22 treated 12 patients via anterior or posterior decompression.
The approach used was based on the location of the compressive pathology. Five of the
12 patients had neurologic deterioration, one of whom had motor function
preoperatively. No attempt at diskectomy was made via the posterior approach. With
more than 2-year follow-up results for all the patients, the authors reported that
outcomes tended to deteriorate with time. In a study of six patients treated via
laminectomy, Barnett et al23 reported more encouraging results. All the patients had
some neurologic improvement; however, these findings are limited by low patient
numbers. Similarly, Smith and Godersky24 reported that all seven patients responded
well neurologically and with regard to pain levels after a laminectomy and facetectomy
for the management of degenerative thoracic stenosis secondary to spondylosis. Follow-
up was less than 1 year in this study. Such narrowing often results from facet
hypertrophy with associated ligamentum buckling. Stenosis also may be developmental;
however, this is less common. Congenital stenosis results from shortened pedicle length
and subsequent decrease in a cross-sectional area of the spinal canal. The degree of
stenosis is best assessed via MRI. In patients with thoracic stenosis, other associated
diagnoses, including ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, ossification of the
yellow ligament, and inflammatory arthridites, must be considered. These conditions
may predispose an individual to stenosis.
Herniation

Herniation
Thoracic level disk herniations are classified based on level and location. Whether a
herniation is calcified is important with regard to surgical management. Thoracic
herniations are considered giant if they involve more than 40% of the spinal canal.25
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM
AAOS | Thoracic Disk Herniations and Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053
6/27

Most herniations are central and occur at the lateral margin of the posterior longitudinal
ligament.19 Most thoracic herniations occur from T8-L1 as the stiffer thoracic spine
transitions to the more mobile lumbar spine and greater degeneration
occurs19,20 (Figure 1). The area of the conus medullaris should be considered because a
herniation at this level may result in unique patient presentations involving bowel and
bladder function. The location of the herniation will determine which neural element
may be compressed. True central herniations are most likely to result in spinal cord
compression and myelopathic findings. Paracentral herniations may result in
compression at the root and/or spinal cord level. Herniations into the foramen will
irritate the respective exiting nerve root.
Calcified herniations are characteristic of thoracic level disease. Although disks may be
soft, calcified disk herniations are more likely to be symptomatic.25 A calcified disk can
adhere to the dura mater and cause tears during resection. Calcified disks are associated
with higher complication rates if managed surgically.25,26 CT should be considered if
concern for calcification exists.
Figure 1 Images of the spine of a 54-year-old man with a 3-week history of severe band-
like pain in the distribution of the T10 dermatome. A, Plain radiograph of the
thoracolumbar junction demonstrates degeneration of the disk spaces, which is

T12-L1 disk (arrow). B, CT myelogram of the T12-L1 disk interspace shows a paramedian
soft disk herniation. The patient had no improvement with nonsurgical treatment and

2000;8[3]:159-169.)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
History and Physical Examination
Thoracic herniations and stenosis are associated with variable patient presentations, including
root and spinal cord level involvement. A thorough evaluation and patient history are critical.
Signs and symptoms may include pain, sensory changes, radiculopathy, and myelopathy.

History and Physical Examination
A complete spine history should be elicited and a complete physical examination should
be performed to ensure correct identification and diagnosis of thoracic-based lesions.
Pain is the most common complaint of patients with symptomatic degenerative
changes.4 Pain from thoracic spinal degeneration is multifactorial and may involve
components of disk, facet, and muscular etiologies. In addition, the relationships
between the facets, disk, ribs, and costovertebral joints may make identification of the
source of pain difficult. Axial-based pain may be disk-based or facet-based and is
transmitted through the medial branch of the dorsal root ganglia, which innervates the
facets, and the sinuvertebral nerve, which innervates the posterior anulus.
In a review of 179 patients, Arce and Dohrman27 reported pain in 57% of the patients,
sensory disturbance in 24% of the patients, motor weakness in 17% of the patients, and
bladder dysfunction in 2% of the patients. Radicular symptoms include band-like pain
that follows a distinct pattern about the chest or abdomen given the involved
dermatomes5 (Figure 2). Depending on the location of the herniation, pain may be
unilateral or bilateral. In some patients, pain may be referred, making identification a

9/4/26, 9:49 AM

8/27

challenge. Lower thoracic herniations may involve symptoms that radiate to the flank,
groin, or legs or symptoms that mimic kidney stones, angina or gastrointestinal
pain.28,29 Herniations at the lower levels of the thoracic spine may compress the conus
or the cauda equina, resulting in leg symptoms and bowel and bladder changes.30
Herniations at the top of the thoracic column may mimic cervical herniations, and
patients may report hand dysfunction, upper extremity pain and numbness, or Horner
syndrome.31
Any history indicative of myelopathy must be explored. Gait changes, hand dysfunction
or clumsiness, fine motor changes, upper or lower extremity weakness, and/or bowel
and bladder dysfunction should be thoroughly investigated.
A comprehensive spinal examination, including evaluation of motor and sensory
function, is critical. Sensory changes may be subtle, and motor weakness may not be
detected because thoracic roots innervate intercostal motor groups. Normal and
abnormal reflexes should be assessed. Long tract signs, including hyperreflexia, the
Babinski sign, sphincter dysfunction, clonus, and ataxia, should be noted. Specific
examination maneuvers, such as flexion of the neck, may reproduce symptoms in
patients with a lower thoracic herniation.32

Imaging Studies
Radiographs
Plain radiographs are less sensitive and are not the preferred imaging study for evaluation.

Imaging Studies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM
AAOS | Thoracic Disk Herniations and Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053
10/27

Plain spine radiographs will demonstrate degenerative changes but are unlikely be
diagnostic unless disk calcification is present. Calcified disks are associated with
herniations, and calcifications within the spinal canal are definitive for diagnosis.3,17,33
Radiographs may aid in evaluating spinal alignment and intervertebral disk
degeneration. Regional kyphosis and Scheuermann disease are associated with an
increased incidence of disk herniation.12,34 Patients with regional kyphosis or
Scheuermann disease may benefit from advanced imaging studies, which allow for
better evaluation of sites of neurologic compression. Instability is rarely observed on
plain radiographs given the stability provided by the ribs.
Advanced Imaging Studies
Myelography
Myelography with plain radiography may aid in localization.
CT myelography is an excellent imaging modality but is associated with radiation exposure.

Myelography
Myelography with radiography is difficult to perform given the kyphotic alignment of the
thoracic spine and the many overlying structures. Myelography with radiography is
associated with a diagnostic accuracy of 56%.7 Myelography should be considered in
patients in whom MRI or CT cannot be obtained. Myelography involves injecting water-
soluble contrast into the lumbar spine, placing the patient in the supine position to allow
the material to migrate and pool in the dependent thoracic canal, and obtaining plain
radiographs.35 The filling of defects helps localize the level of compression. CT
myelography affords excellent visualization of thoracic herniations and may provide
information with regard to intradural penetration.4,35,36 CT allows for better
characterization of bony structures and evaluation for a calcified thoracic disk, ossified
ligamentum flavum, or ossified posterior longitudinal ligament.
Magnetic resonance imaging
MRI allows for excellent characterization of thoracic compression (Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053

Bony and soft-tissue structures can be imaged effectively.
MRI may result in the overdiagnosis of thoracic disk herniations.
Thoracic MRI allows for better characterization of disk herniations and stenosis. MRI is
quick, effective, and noninvasive, and is not associated with radiation exposure. The
sensitivity of MRI is similar to that of CT.37 Axial, coronal, and parasagittal views of the
thoracic spine can be obtained to characterize sites of neural compression.35,38 MRI also
allows for visualization of the spinal cord and the surrounding soft tissue, including
disks, ligaments, and musculature. Contrast can be used to better define disk material in
the spinal canal because it will not enhance.
Although MRI has revolutionized imaging of the thoracic spine, the interpretation of
MRIs, may be a challenge. Cardiac motion, pulsatile movement of blood and spinal fluid,
bone marrow, and calcifications may contribute to decreased accuracy of MRI.37-39 In
addition, MRI findings of thoracic stenosis and disk herniation must be interpreted
carefully because they are observed in 30% of asymptomatic individuals.12

Management

A trial of nonsurgical treatment should be the first-line treatment option for patients with
thoracic disk herniations and stenosis who do not have signs and symptoms of neurologic
compression.
Surgical treatment is reserved for patients with myelopathy, patients with weakness, patients
with pain in whom nonsurgical management fails, and patients with bowel and bladder
dysfunction.
Nonsurgical Management
Most patients with a thoracic disk herniation are asymptomatic and should be treated
nonsurgically. Indications for surgical management include persistent pain in a radicular
pattern that fails to respond to nonsurgical management, myelopathy, weakness or paralysis,
and bowel or bladder dysfunction. Most patients with radicular complaints improve after a
trial on nonsurgical treatment and physical therapy.5 A standard treatment regimen may
include core strengthening, physical therapy, and appropriate exercise and stretching.
Medications, such as NSAIDs, may be considered unless contraindicated, such as in patients
with renal or gastrointestinal comorbidities. Oral steroids may be considered but only for
short-term management. In general, narcotics are not recommended. Short-term bracing may
be attempted; however, long-term bracing is not recommended.
Indications
Asymptomatic disk herniations and stenosis with no evidence of myelopathy
Axial back pain
New radicular symptoms without progressive motor weakness and sensory changes (trial of
nonsurgical management)
Contraindications
Indications for surgical management include persistent pain in a radicular pattern that fails to
respond to nonsurgical management, myelopathy, weakness or paralysis, and bowel or
bladder dysfunction.
Techniques/Procedures

Nonsurgical management involves physical therapy, NSAIDs, core strengthening, stretching,
and activity modifications.
Outcomes
Most patients with radicular complaints improved after a trial of nonsurgical treatment and
physical therapy.5

Outcomes
A study by Brown et al5 reported that 77% of patients with radiculopathy as the primary
complaint improved after a trial of nonsurgical treatment and physical therapy.
Nonsurgical treatment should always be considered in patients without progressive
deficits or myelopathy.
Surgical Management
The goals of surgical management include decompression of neural elements without
manipulation of the spinal cord.
Laminectomy alone has limited to no role
Multiple approaches are available based on the location of the compression and regional
anatomy.
Fusion should be considered in patients in whom the spine may be destabilized during the
approach.
In patients with thoracic stenosis, posterior pathology is best managed via posterior surgery,
including laminectomy and foraminotomy. Alignment is critical because aggressive kyphosis
may not be adequately decompressed via a posterior technique alone.
Indications
Surgical management should be considered for pain that fails to respond to nonsurgical
management, myelopathy, weakness, or bowel and bladder dysfunction.


Indications
Surgical management for the aforementioned indications results in the best outcomes;
therefore, surgeons should adhere to strict indications. Available surgical techniques
have advanced considerably since early procedures involving laminectomy alone. An
early review reported that, after laminectomy for the management of herniated thoracic
disks, 28% of patients had worse pathology, 58% of patients had improved pathology,
10% of patients had unchanged pathology, and 4% of patients died.27 The goals of
surgical management include spinal cord and root level decompression and removal of
offending pathology. Early treatment is ideal for patients with myelopathy; however,
good results can be obtained in patients with an extended time to diagnosis.36
Myelopathy from ossified structures adjacent to the spinal cord portends a poorer
outcome.40 Laminectomy alone is of very limited use for the management of ventral
lesions and may be contraindicated.41,42
Disk excision
No preferred approach exists for the excision of a herniated thoracic disk. Adequate access to
the spinal canal is required to allow for safe, wide decompression of neural elements. Spinal
cord manipulation should be minimized or, ideally, avoided completely. Advanced imaging
studies may allow for detailed surgical planning based on regional anatomy and the location of
compression.
Fusion
Fusion with instrumentation after thoracic disk excision is indicated if the spinal stability has
been altered. Fusion is not necessary if only a small portion of disk or bone is removed;
however, fusion is recommended if extensive facetectomy or rib resection is performed.
Fusion is indicated in patients who undergo complete diskectomy.36 Spondylolisthesis or
kyphosis, such as in patients with Scheuermann disease, should be noted because such
findings also are indications for fusion.18 Although recurrent thoracic disk herniations have not
been reported, fusion theoretically prevents this complication. The decision to fuse the

thoracic spine should be based on the degree of instability introduced intraoperatively, the
degree of preoperative kyphosis or alignment variables, and the degree of preoperative
instability.
Techniques/Procedures
Posterior-Based Surgical Management
Costotransversectomy
Transpedicular access
Transfacet access

Posterior-Based Surgical Management
For stenosis and lateral and paracentral disk herniations, posterior-based approaches to
the spine are common and familiar to surgeons (Figure 4). An approach surgeon often is
not required, and access to the thoracic cavity rarely is indicated, obviating the need for
a chest tube. Access to the ventral spinal cord and canal is possible, and posterior-based
approaches allow for excellent visualization of the neural foramen.
Figure 4 Schematic drawings show comparison of the relative exposures (diagonal lines)

17/27

provided by five surgical approaches: laminectomy (A), transpedicular (B),
costotransversectomy (C), lateral extracavitary (D), and transthoracic (E). As the exposure
angle becomes more anterior and visualization of the ventral structures improves, the
amount of dissection increases. (Reproduced from Gebhauer G, Vaccaro A: Thoracic disk
herniation and stenosis, in Rao RD, Smuck M, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine,
ed 4. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2012, pp 324-328.)
Costotransversectomy is a technique to access the ventral spinal canal and facilitates
removal of central and lateral disk material.18,43 The patient is placed in the prone
position, and a standard posterior-based approach is used to raise paraspinal muscle
flaps.44 The posterior portion of the rib or ribs at the appropriate level on the side of the
herniation can be excised. The rib head and neck and the transverse process are
removed. Care should be taken to remain extrapleural, limiting morbidity and the need
for a chest tube. The corresponding intercostal nerve can be traced to its exiting site
through the foramen to aid in identification of the neural foramen and to access the
spinal canal. A portion of the pedicle is removed to allow for ventral access to the spinal
canal without direct manipulation of the spinal cord. This provides access to the disk
herniation. Certain anatomic considerations, such as the body habitus of the patient and
the location of the aorta, may limit access via this approach.
Transpedicular access involves a posterior approach with removal of the ipsilateral
pedicle and facet to expose the spinal canal16 (Figure 5) True central herniations may be
a challenge to access via the transpedicular approach. Instruments that afford access the
ventral spinal cord, such as angled or reverse angled curettes, are necessary. Le Roux et
al10 reported excellent results in 20 patients who were treated via the transpedicular
approach for the management of a lateral or central disk herniation.
Transfacet access involves the creation of a window through the facet joint at the level
and side of the disk herniation. Foraminal disk herniations are best accessed via this
approach.32 The periphery of the facet can be preserved, maintaining some inherent
stability, and fusion may not be necessary for single-level surgical procedures. A
modified technique involves removal of the entire facet.16 Other advantages of the
transfacet approach include decreased blood loss and shorter surgical times. Central
decompression may be limited, and the working window may be small given the body
habitus of the patient. Stillerman et al9 reported on a transfacet pedicle-sparing

Anterior-Based Surgical Management
Transthoracic approach
Video-assisted thoracoscopic approach
Minimally invasive approach

Anterior-Based Surgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:49 AM
AAOS | Thoracic Disk Herniations and Stenosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000053
19/27

Advantages of anterior-based procedures include more direct access to the
spinal canal and disk space, better access to central herniations, direct
visualization of ventral compressive pathology, and improved access and
visualization of intradural pathology. Disadvantages of anterior-based
procedures primarily include morbidity from the exposure, including vascular
and pulmonary injury, and spinal cord ischemia. A chest tube is required if a
thoracotomy is performed. Dual lumen intubation is necessary because the lung
must be collapsed on the side of the surgical procedure. Diaphragmatic hernias
also are potential complications after access to the lower thoracic spine.
Foraminal access is limited.
Spinal cord ischemia, which is a devastating complication, is a known risk factor
associated with anterior approaches. The aorta and the spinal segmental
vessels are positioned across the surgical field during exposure; therefore, great
care must be taken to limit mobilization. The watershed area between T4-T9 is
supplied by the artery of Adamkiewicz. This vessel travels on the left side in 80%
of patients, supplying the spinal cord. Although some studies recommend
preoperative angiography to determine the location of major feeding vessels in
relation to a disk herniation, careful dissection obviates the need for
preoperative angiography.45-48
Transthoracic decompression is an alternative to costotransversectomy but is a
more direct approach to the spinal column, particularly from T4-T12. The
transthoracic approach offers better visualization and affords access to the
ventral spinal canal. Risks associated with the transthoracic approach include
complications associated with a thoracotomy.4,37,46,47 Bohlman and Zdeblick36
reported the outcomes of 19 patients with a thoracic disk herniation who
underwent costotransversectomy or transthoracic decompression. The authors
recommended transthoracic decompression as the preferred strategy for the
management of thoracic disk herniations given the superior visualization
afforded via the transthoracic approach. Reported results included one patient
with myelopathy who did not have neurologic improvement after
costotransversectomy. Two patients who underwent costotransversectomy had
transient paraparesis.

For the transthoracic approach, the patient is placed in the lateral decubitus
position. Consideration should be made for the level of the herniation because
the liver may make access difficult lower in the thoracic spine. The aorta is more
easily mobilized than the vena cava, making a transthoracic approach on the left
side more favorable than that on the right side.37,46 A rib is resected to aid in
exposure; this can be planned based on the appropriate overlying rib. A partial
corpectomy may be performed to afford better visualization and access to the
offending disk. Alternatively, diskectomy alone can be performed; however, this
may be technically challenging.34,37,46 Manipulation of the spinal cord must be
avoided.
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is an alternative approach for access to
problematic thoracic disk herniations. Initially described in the early 1990s, the
video-assisted thoracoscopic approach has been refined, and several large
series on the video-assisted thoracoscopic approach have reported good
patient outcomes.11,48-51 Advantages of the video-assisted thoracoscopic
approach include avoidance of many of the complications associated with a
thoracotomy, improved visualization, decreased postoperative pain, and shorter
rehabilitation and hospitalization. Studies also have advocated thoracoscopic
approaches to avoid the complications associated with open thoracotomy.
Multiple portals and cannula are used, and two surgeons can work in tandem.
Disadvantages of the video-assisted thoracoscopic approach include a steep
learning curve and the need for specialized thoracoscopic instruments and
postoperative intercostal neuralgia. Relative contraindications to the video-
assisted thoracoscopic approach include pleural adhesions, a prior chest tube,
and respiratory insufficiency.
More recently, tubular dilators have been used to afford minimally invasive
access to the thoracic spine. Initially trialed in cadaver models, the minimally
invasive approach has translated well in the operating room, with multiple
series reporting strong patient outcomes.52-55 Similar to the video-assisted
thoracoscopic approach, the goal of the minimally invasive approach is to
achieve thoracic decompression without the morbidity associated with large,
open posterior approaches or thoracotomies. In addition, fusion is less likely

with the minimally invasive approach. A benefit of tubular surgery is direct
visualization of the surgical field without lung deflation. Patients are placed in
the lateral decubitus position, and the thoracic spine is accessed from the
retropleural space. Fluoroscopy aids in identifying the appropriate level, and
ribs often are spread rather than resected.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Asymptomatic thoracic disk herniations can be managed nonsurgically.
A careful patient history and physical examination may provide critical details regarding the
signs and symptoms of myelopathy.
Nonsurgical management includes physical therapy and activity modifications.
Indications for surgical management include pain unresponsive to nonsurgical management,
myelopathy, weakness, and bowel and bladder dysfunction.
The best surgical results are observed if indications are strictly followed.
Anterior, posterior, and minimally invasive approaches are viable options. The approach
selected should be based on the location of the pathology and surgeon preference.
